text: Sadler's Wells Theatre opens in London.
Ulster Canal abandoned.
Winston Churchill resigns from Stanley Baldwin's shadow cabinet after disagreeing with the policy of conciliation with Indian nationalism.
for the fourth time in nine years, there is a fatal underground explosion at Haig Pit, Whitehaven, in the Cumberland Coalfield, killing 27 people.

RAF Blackburn Iris III seaplane S 238 crashes in Plymouth Sound after a senior officer takes control from the pilot and fails to make a safe landing, resulting in multiple fatalities. One of the first to the rescue is T. E. Lawrence, stationed locally at this time.
Oswald Mosley forms the New Party, having resigned from the Labour Party a day earlier.

Westminster St George's by-election results in the victory of the Conservative candidate Duff Cooper. The by-election has been treated virtually as a referendum on the leadership of the Conservative leader Stanley Baldwin, and Duff Cooper's victory ends the campaign by the press barons Lord Beaverbrook and Viscount Rothermere to oust Baldwin.
the Highway Code first issued.
census in England, Wales and Scotland.
National Trust for Scotland established and acquires its first property, Crookston Castle.
the Vic-Wells Ballet, later to become The Royal Ballet, debuts in London.
shoppers in London escape with their lives when a chemical factory in Bayswater explodes.
Whipsnade Zoo is opened in Bedfordshire by the Zoological Society of London.

publication of Report of the Committee on Finance and Industry (the 'Macmillan Committee') on the relationship between the banking and financial system and British trade and industry, largely written by John Maynard Keynes.
the Dogger Bank earthquake is felt across Britain.
submarine sinks after collision with a Chinese freighter off Weihai, China. Twenty lives are lost but a few submariners become the first to surface using the Davis Submerged Escape Apparatus.
new Royal Corinthian Yacht Club clubhouse at Burnham-on-Crouch in Essex, a pioneering British example of International Style designed by Joseph Emberton, is opened.

the May Report of the Committee on National Expenditure recommends extensive cuts in government spending. This produces a political crisis as many members of the Labour Party government object to the proposals.
a run on the pound leads to a political and economic crisis in Britain, part of the European banking crisis of 1931.
Labour Government of Ramsay MacDonald resigns and is replaced by a National Government of people drawn from all parties also under MacDonald, as suggested by King George V earlier in the year.
John Thomson, goalkeeper of Celtic, dies in hospital after fracturing his skull in a collision with Rangers forward Sam English in the 'Old Firm' League derby at Ibrox Park.
Chancellor of the Exchequer Philip Snowden announces salary cuts for all government employees and reductions to unemployment benefit.

second Round Table Conference on the constitutional future of India opens in London. Mahatma Gandhi represents the Indian National Congress and on the weekend of 26 September visits the Lancashire cotton town of Darwen.

Schneider Trophy seaplane race flown at Calshot Spit. For the third successive time the British team (sponsored by Lady Houston) wins with Flt. Lt. John Boothman flying the course in Supermarine S.6B serial S1595 designed by R. J. Mitchell with Rolls-Royce R engines at a world record speed of 340.09 mph (547.31 km/h). On 29 September Flt Lt. George Stainforth in S.6B serial S1596 breaks
Invergordon Mutiny: Strikes in the Royal Navy as a result of pay cuts.
pound sterling comes off the gold standard.
MI5 ceases to be a section of the War Office, being officially renamed the Security Service, and takes over the counter-subversion section (SSI) from Scotland Yard's Special Branch.
Leeds Bradford International Airport is opened as Leeds and Bradford Municipal Aerodrome.

general election results in victory for the National Government in the country's greatest ever electoral landslide. Ramsay MacDonald remains Prime Minister. This election is held on a Tuesday: all subsequent ones will be held on Thursdays.
Abbey Road Studios in London are opened by Sir Edward Elgar.
an underground firedamp explosion at Bentley Colliery in the South Yorkshire Coalfield kills 45.
the infamous Red-and-White Party, given by Arthur Jeffress in Maud Allan's Regent's Park town house in London, marks the end of the "Bright young things" subculture in Britain.

Parliament enacts the Statute of Westminster, which establishes a status of legislative equality between the self-governing dominions of the Commonwealth of Australia, Canada, the Irish Free State, Newfoundland, the Dominion of New Zealand and the Union of South Africa.
Great Depression: work on construction of "Hull Number 534", the future ocean liner , at John Brown & Company's shipyard on Clydebank is suspended for more than two years.
the statue of Eros returns to London's Piccadilly Circus after a nine-year absence.
Ministry of Health encourages local councils to engage in widespread slum clearance.
John Cockcroft and Ernest Walton, at the Cavendish Laboratory in the University of Cambridge, focus a proton beam on lithium and split its nucleus ("splitting the atom").
India plays its first Test cricket match with England at Lord's.
George Lansbury becomes the leader of the opposition Labour Party.
The London Underground diagram designed by Harry Beck is introduced to the public.
The King and Country debate: The Oxford Union student debating society passes a resolution stating, "That this House will in no circumstances fight for its King and country."
English cricket team in Australia in 1932–33: Tour concludes with the England cricket team winning The Ashes using the controversial bodyline tactic.
First car race at Donington Park circuit in Leicestershire.

1933 Imperial Airways Dixmude crash: The Imperial Airways Armstrong Whitworth Argosy biplane airliner City of Liverpool catches fire in the air over Belgium and crashes, killing the crew of three and all twelve passengers, the deadliest accident in the history of British civil aviation to this date. The fire onboard may have been started deliberately.
As a member of the English cricket team touring New Zealand, 1933, batsman Wally Hammond scores a record 336 runs in a test match at Eden Park, Auckland.
The Marquess of Douglas and Clydesdale leads an expedition to be the first to fly an aircraft over Mount Everest.

Children and Young Persons Act 1933 passed. This raises the age of criminal responsibility from 7 to 8, raises the minimum age for capital punishment to 18, places restrictions on the identification in the press of persons under 18 appearing in court, sets a minimum full-time working age of 14 with other limitations on the employment of school-age children, and makes it illegal for adults to sell
The Jessop & Son department store in Nottingham is acquired by the John Lewis Partnership, its first store outside London.

First air service internal to Scotland, Renfrew–Campbeltown, operated by Midland & Scottish Air Ferries Ltd. Winifred Drinkwater, "the world's first female commercial pilot", is hired to fly the route.
First modern "sighting" of the Loch Ness Monster.
London Passenger Transport Board begins operations, unifying multiple earlier services by road and Underground.
New Chiswick Bridge, Twickenham Bridge and Hampton Court Bridge over the River Thames are officially opened.
Signing of the Four-Power Pact by the UK, France, Germany and Italy.
Battersea Power Station, London, first generates electricity.
Grand jury abolished in English law.
Winston Churchill makes his first public speech warning of the dangers of German rearmament.
Release of the film The Private Life of Henry VIII. Charles Laughton receives an Academy Award for the title rôle (16 March 1934), making this the first British film to win an Oscar.
National Grid completed.
Milk Marketing Board established.
British Interplanetary Society founded in Liverpool.
The Rolls-Royce Merlin aircraft engine is run for the first time (on bench test in Derby).
Birmingham city council's 40,000th council house (on the Weoley Castle estate) is opened by Chancellor of the Exchequer Neville Chamberlain.
George Eyston achieves a world land speed record for a diesel car of 101.98 mph (164.12 km/h) at Brooklands.
Establishment of the National Council for Civil Liberties by Ronald Kidd and Sylvia Crowther-Smith.
Ten thousand people attend a British Union of Fascists rally in Birmingham, organised by Oswald Mosley.
A Commission of Government for the Dominion of Newfoundland is sworn in as a form of return to direct colonial rule by the UK forced by the island's economic collapse.

The Betting and Lotteries Act 1934 is passed. Part 1 (betting) is designed to restrict betting on racecourses and tracks to a maximum of 104 days. Part 2 (lotteries) prohibits the sale of lottery tickets, primarily directed against the Irish Free State Hospitals' Sweepstake.
Meccano Ltd introduce the first Dinky Toys.
Percy Shaw patents the cat's eye road-safety device.
Rudyard Kipling and William Butler Yeats are awarded the Gothenburg Prize for Poetry.
The London Zoo penguin pool, designed by Berthold Lubetkin's Tecton Architectural Group with Ove Arup, one of the most significant examples of modern architecture in Britain, is opened.
54-year-old grandmother Mrs G. E. Alington becomes the first woman in Britain to complete a parachute jump, skydiving from 1500 feet over Brooklands Aerodrome.
Opening of the first Glyndebourne Festival Opera season.
First regular domestic airmail service, inaugurated by Highland Airways between Inverness and Kirkwall.
Petroleum (Production) Act vests ownership of all U.K. subterranean oil and natural gas in the Crown.
Opening of the Queensway Tunnel beneath the River Mersey by King George V.
41 squadrons added to the Royal Air Force as part of a new air defence program.
British Empire Games held at Wembley Park, London.
The BBC's most powerful long-wave transmitter, Droitwich Transmitting Station, starts transmitting regularly at 200 kilohertz, following test transmissions from 8 May.
The British Graham Land Expedition sets out to explore Graham Land in Antarctica.

Gresford disaster: a gas explosion takes place at Gresford Colliery in Wrexham, north-east Wales, which leads to the death of 266 miners and rescuers, one of the worst tragedies in Welsh mining history.
Launch of the liner at Clydebank.
Stanley Matthews makes his debut for the England national football team, beginning a record 23-year international career.

Marriage of Prince George, Duke of Kent, to Princess Marina of Greece and Denmark, the first this century, and last, foreign-born princess to marry into the British royal family; the wedding is the first to be broadcast live on radio.
London and North Eastern Railway steam locomotive Class A3 4472 Flying Scotsman becomes the first officially to exceed 100 miles per hour (160.9 km/h) on test in England.
Arthur Henderson wins the Nobel Peace Prize.
Special Areas Act provides grants from central government funds to assist regions with high unemployment.
Ramblers' Association founded.
the Rolls-Royce Merlin aircraft engine is first flown, at Hucknall Aerodrome.
Robert Watson-Watt first demonstrates the use of radar, at Daventry.
King Prajadhipok (Rama VII) of Siam abdicates and flees with his wife Rambai Barni to England.
Croydon Aerodrome robbery: £21,000 worth of gold is stolen and never recovered.
speed limit in built-up areas reduced to 30 mph.
Britain protests at Germany's introduction of conscription.
reflective cat's-eyes first used on British roads.
The British Empire holds silver jubilee celebrations for King George V.
Ewart Astill captains Leicestershire County Cricket Club for the remainder of the season, the first professional cricketer to lead any county on a regular basis since the 19th century.

Arabist, historian and war hero T. E. Lawrence, known as Lawrence of Arabia, is involved in a serious accident while riding his motorcycle near Clouds Hill, his home in Dorset; he dies of his injuries on 19 May, aged 46.

Northamptonshire County Cricket Club gains (over Somerset at Taunton by 48 runs) what proves to be their last victory for 99 matches, easily a record in the County Championship. Their next Championship win will not be until 29 May 1939.
canonization of Cardinal John Fisher and Sir Thomas More by Pope Pius XI. This year also, Bede is sanctified by the Catholic Church.
the funeral of T. E. Lawrence is held at St Nicholas' Church, Moreton in Dorset. Winston Churchill, E. M. Forster, Lady Astor and King Ghazi of Iraq attend.
the government announces plans to triple the size of the Royal Air Force in the next two years, partly in response to German re-armament.
Woolmington v DPP, a landmark case decided on appeal in the House of Lords, reaffirms the presumption of innocence as the "golden thread" in criminal law.
the driving test becomes compulsory.
Alfred Hitchcock's film of The 39 Steps released in the UK.
Ramsay MacDonald retires; Stanley Baldwin takes over as prime minister.
Anglo-German Naval Agreement: Britain agrees to a German navy equal to 35% of her own naval tonnage.
first portion of Swanscombe skull, belonging to a woman from 400,000 years past, is discovered in north Kent.

rioting breaks out in Belfast following Orange parades; by the end of August eight Protestants and five Catholics have been killed, hundreds injured and over 2,000 homes destroyed (almost all Catholic).

official completion of the London County Council's Becontree estate in East London, the largest housing estate in the world, consisting of some 27,000 new council houses which are home to more than 100,000 people. The first families moved to the estate, which straddles the borders of Dagenham, Barking and Ilford, in 1921.
T. E. Lawrence's Seven Pillars of Wisdom is first published in an edition for general circulation, two months after his death resulting from a motorcycle accident.
Allen Lane founds Penguin Books to publish the first mass market paperbacks in Britain.
the Deaflympics take place in London.
last service held in Mardale church in the Lake District prior to the village's flooding to create Manchester Corporation's Haweswater Reservoir.
Malcolm Campbell breaks the 300 mph barrier for the first time and sets a new land speed record of at the Bonneville Salt Flats, Utah, driving the Campbell-Railton Blue Bird.
Bahram completes the English Triple Crown by finishing first in the 2,000 Guineas, Epsom Derby and St Leger.
an underground explosion at North Gawber (Lidgett) colliery, Barnsley, South Yorkshire, kills nineteen.

the London and North Eastern Railway begins to run the Silver Jubilee train between London King's Cross and Newcastle, Britain's first streamliner, using Nigel Gresley's LNER Class A4 steam locomotives.
first steel produced from new works at Corby.
Clement Attlee is appointed as interim leader of the Labour Party in succession to George Lansbury who has resigned due to a wish to maintain his Christian pacifist principles.
Grant v Australian Knitting Mills, a landmark case in consumer law, decided on appeal in the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council.
opening of Hornsey Town Hall, London, designed by Reginald Uren, the first major UK building in the International Style.
maiden flight of the Royal Air Force's Hawker Hurricane fighter aircraft, at Brooklands.

in the general election, Prime Minister Stanley Baldwin is returned to office at the head of a National Government led by the Conservative Party with a large but reduced majority. This election begins the modern tradition of the Speaker of the House of Commons seeking re-election as such rather than under a party label. There will be no further general election for 10 years.
opening of The De La Warr Pavilion at Bexhill on Sea in East Sussex, designed by Erich Mendelsohn and Serge Chermayeff in the International style.
Samuel Hoare resigns as foreign secretary; replaced by Anthony Eden.
England celebrates its first ever win over the All Blacks in rugby union, in particular the two famous tries by "The Prince" HH Alexander Obolensky.
GPO Film Unit documentary Night Mail, incorporating poetry by W. H. Auden and music by Benjamin Britten, is premiered at the Cambridge Arts Theatre.
King George V dies at Sandringham House, Norfolk, aged 70. His eldest son, Edward, Prince of Wales succeeds as King Edward VIII.
King Edward VIII breaks royal protocol by watching the proclamation of his own accession to the throne from a window of St. James's Palace, in the company of the still-married Wallis Simpson.
John Maynard Keynes's influential economic text The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money is published.
Great Britain and Northern Ireland compete at the Winter Olympics in Garmisch-Partenkirchen, Germany, and win 1 gold, 1 silver and 1 bronze medals.
First test flight of the Supermarine Spitfire, from Eastleigh Aerodrome.
K6 red telephone box introduced, together with GPO 'Jubilee concession' to provide one in every village with a post office.
Billy Butlin opens his first Butlins holiday camp, Butlins Skegness in Skegness (Ingoldmells), Lincolnshire. It is officially opened by Amy Johnson.
Ordnance Survey begins the retriangulation of Great Britain with its first triangulation station near Cold Ashby, Northamptonshire.
Barquentine Waterwitch is laid up at Par, Cornwall, the last square rigged ship to trade under sail alone in British ownership.
J. H. Thomas resigns from politics for leaking Budget proposals.
The leaves Southampton on her maiden voyage to New York.
Alan Turing submits his paper "On Computable Numbers" to the London Mathematical Society for publication, introducing the concept of the "Turing machine". It is formally published on 12 November.
George McMahon makes a botched attempt to shoot King Edward VIII after the Trooping the Colour ceremony.
The General Post Office introduces the speaking clock.
Charlotte Bryant is hanged at HM Prison Exeter for the murder of her husband Frederick by arsenic in Dorset.
Opening of a new swimming pool at Morecambe, claimed to be the largest open-air example in Europe.
Great Britain wins the 1936 International Lawn Tennis Challenge at Wimbledon, the last British victory until 2015 in what becomes the Davis Cup.
Public Health Act empowers local authorities to make byelaws regulating building construction.
September – Bournemouth typhoid outbreak: more than 700 people infected.
Great Britain and Northern Ireland compete at the Olympics in Berlin and win 4 gold, 7 silver and 3 bronze medals.
The Duke of Grafton is killed in a crash while competing in the Limerick Grand Prix in Ireland, aged only 22. His cousin succeeds to the main title, but the courtesy titles fall into abeyance.
An underground explosion at Wharncliffe Woodmoor Colliery in South Yorkshire kills 58.
Signing of the Anglo-Egyptian Treaty which requires the withdrawal of British troops and recognises Egypt as a sovereign state.
Elizabeth Cowell becomes the first female British television presenter, making a broadcast from Alexandra Palace.

Arson attack on a bombing school building at Penyberth on the Llŷn Peninsula as part of the Tân yn Llŷn campaign led by Saunders Lewis, Lewis Valentine and D. J. Williams of the Welsh nationalist group Plaid Genedlaethol Cymru.
Official opening of Pinewood Studios.
Battle of Cable Street between Oswald Mosley's British Union of Fascists and anti-fascist demonstrators in the East End of London.
The Night Ferry, a boat train service linking London with Paris, starts operation.
Jarrow March: 207 miners march from Jarrow to London in a protest against unemployment and poverty.
Prime minister Stanley Baldwin confronts King Edward VIII about his relationship with Wallis Simpson.
Dod Orsborne, captain of the fishing vessel Girl Pat, which had caused a media sensation when it went missing, is convicted of its theft and given a prison sentence.
Wallis Simpson obtains a decree nisi in her divorce from Ernest Aldrich Simpson, removing a legal barrier to her marrying Edward VIII.

The BBC launches the world's first regular television service in London, initially alternating between the 240-line Baird electromechanical and the Marconi-EMI all-electronic 405-line television systems.
The State Opening of Parliament is held; it is Edward VIII's only state opening. The ceremonial procession is cancelled due to heavy rain.
Terence Rattigan's comedy French Without Tears premieres in London.
Alan Turing's paper "On Computable Numbers" is formally presented to the London Mathematical Society, introducing the concept of the "Turing machine".

King Edward VIII informs Stanley Baldwin of his intention to marry Wallis Simpson. Baldwin responds by informing the King that any woman he married would have to become Queen, and the British public would not accept Wallis Simpson as Queen. The King tells Mr Baldwin that he is prepared to abdicate if the government opposes his marriage.

The King tells Stanley Baldwin that he would be prepared to conduct a morganatic marriage with Mrs Simpson, which would allow him to carry on as King but not install Mrs Simpson as Queen. Stanley Baldwin informs him that this would not be accepted either (such a thing has never been known in British law).
Stanley Baldwin raises the issue of a morganatic marriage in the Cabinet, where it is rejected outright.
The Crystal Palace in south London is destroyed in a fire.
Henry Hallett Dale wins the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine jointly with Otto Loewi "for their discoveries relating to chemical transmission of nerve impulses".
Alfred Blunt, Bishop of Bradford, makes a speech which inadvertently leads to the abdication crisis becoming public in the British media.
Stanley Baldwin confirms in a meeting with the King that a morganatic marriage would not be accepted, and in order to marry Mrs Simpson the King would have to abdicate.

A KLM (Netherlands airline) Douglas DC-2 airliner crashes in Purley shortly after takeoff from Croydon Airport, killing 14 (including Juan de la Cierva and Admiral Arvid Lindman) with just two survivors.
Abdication crisis: the King signs an instrument of abdication at Fort Belvedere in the presence of his three brothers, The Duke of York, The Duke of Gloucester and The Duke of Kent.
Public Order Act prevents wearing of political uniforms with effect from 1 January next.

Princess Alexandra of Kent, daughter of The Duke and Duchess of Kent, is born in London. This will be the last royal birth attended by the Home Secretary, in this case, John Simon, 1st Viscount Simon.
safety glass in vehicle windscreens becomes mandatory in the United Kingdom.
UK première of the historical film Fire Over England, providing the first pairing of Laurence Olivier and Vivien Leigh.
Prince Edward, the former King Edward VIII, is created Duke of Windsor.
Regency Act 1937 provides for the minority, incapacity or absence abroad of any future monarch.
Frank Whittle ground-tests the world's first jet engine designed to power an aircraft, at Rugby.
National Maritime Museum opened at Greenwich in former Royal Hospital School premises.
the Royal Mint introduces the twelve-sided nickel-brass threepence coin, superseding the earlier round silver coin.
the Georgian Group is set up as part of the Society for the Protection of Ancient Buildings in England.
London's bus drivers and conductors go on strike.

Coronation of George VI and Elizabeth takes place at Westminster Abbey, London. The BBC makes its first television outside broadcast covering the event. The newly formed social research organisation Mass Observation makes its first survey of social attitudes on this day.
nearly 4000 Basque (and other) child refugees of the Spanish Civil War arrive at Southampton.
George VI passes letters patent denying the style of Royal Highness to the wife and descendants of the Duke of Windsor.
Neville Chamberlain becomes Prime Minister after Baldwin's retirement.
the Duke of Windsor marries Wallis Simpson in the Château de Candé.
Holditch Colliery Disaster, a coal mining accident in Chesterton, Staffordshire, in which thirty men die following a fire and explosions.
Littlewoods, the pools company formed fourteen years ago by Liverpool businessman John Moores, expands to create a department store in Blackpool, Lancashire.
Peel Commission proposes partition of the British Mandate of Palestine into separate Arab and Jewish states.
Matrimonial Causes Act adds insanity and desertion to infidelity as legitimate grounds for divorce.
assassination attempt on King George VI in Belfast by the Irish Republican Army.
return of the British Graham Land Expedition from Antarctica.
Benjamin Britten's string orchestral work Variations on a Theme of Frank Bridge, Op. 10, receives its concert première at the Salzburg Festival, bringing the composer to international attention.
Witley Court in Worcestershire is gutted by fire.
last issue of The Morning Post newspaper before it is absorbed by The Daily Telegraph.
December – Croydon typhoid outbreak of 1937: 341 cases of typhoid fever (43 fatal) result from a polluted well.
the fictional character 'Mrs. Miniver' first appears in the column on domestic life written by 'Jan Struther' for The Times.
Jimmy McGrory plays his last match with Celtic F.C., achieving a United Kingdom record of 550 goals scored during his senior career.
the first issue of children's comic The Dandy, including the character Desperate Dan, is published.
the musical Me and My Girl opens in the West End Victoria Palace Theatre; the dance number "The Lambeth Walk" becomes popular.
The Hawker Hurricane enters service with the Royal Air Force as its first monoplane fighter aircraft (with No. 111 Squadron at Northolt).
Sir Alexander Cadogan succeeds Sir Robert Vansittart as permanent under-secretary at the Foreign Office.
Joseph P. Kennedy Sr., is appointed United States Ambassador to the United Kingdom.
The British naval base at Singapore begins operations.
Anthony Eden resigns as Foreign Secretary over the foreign policy of the Chamberlain ministry towards Fascist Italy. Lord Halifax takes over.

Chamberlain makes a speech in the House of Commons saying the government "emphatically" disapproves of the Nazi German Anschluss in Austria two days previously but that "nothing could have prevented this action by Germany unless we and others with us had been prepared to use force to prevent it."
Anglo-Italian Treaty: Britain recognises Italian government over Ethiopia, in return for Italian troops withdrawing from Spain.
York Castle Museum opened.
Anglo-Irish Trade Agreement with the Republic of Ireland settles the Anglo-Irish Trade War and agrees to the Royal Navy abandoning the British sovereign bases at the Treaty ports in Ireland.
Empire Exhibition opens in Glasgow.
An underground explosion at Markham Colliery, near Staveley, Derbyshire, kills 79.
The Bren light machine gun comes into service with the British Army.
The children's zoo at London Zoo is opened by Robert and Ted Kennedy, two of the sons of United States ambassador Joseph P. Kennedy.
Women's Voluntary Service founded to assist the Civil Defence Service.
Test cricket is televised for the first time.
The London and North Eastern Railway's streamlined Class A4 4468 Mallard reaches a speed of 126 mph (203 km/h), the highest certified speed for a steam locomotive.
Gas masks are issued to the civilian population.

3 October – Military installations at the Treaty Ports in the Republic of Ireland (Berehaven, Spike Island at Queenstown, and Lough Swilly) are handed over from British control to the Government of Ireland, under terms of the Anglo-Irish Trade Agreement ratified by the Eire (Confirmation of Agreements) Act earlier in the year.

Britain rejects a proposal from its ambassador in Berlin, Nevile Henderson, for a four power summit on Czechoslovakia consisting of Britain, France, Germany and the U.S.S.R. as London will under no circumstances accept the Soviet Union as a diplomatic partner.
Holidays with Pay Act provides for paid annual leave in wage-regulated industries and for similar voluntary schemes in other employment.
The Beano comic first goes on sale, featuring the character Lord Snooty.
Muslims protest in London about passages they consider disrespectful of their religion in H. G. Wells' A Short History of the World (1922).
Lord Runciman, sent by Neville Chamberlain, arrives in Prague on his mission of mediation in the Sudetenland dispute.
Major thunderstorm over Devon.
Great Britain and the United States contest the inaugural Amateur World Series in baseball, played in the north of England. Britain wins every match.

Ewald von Kleist-Schmenzin arrives in London looking for British support for an anti-Nazi putsch, using the looming crisis over the Sudetenland as a pretext. His private mission is dismissed by Neville Chamberlain as unimportant (Chamberlain refers to von Kleist as a "Jacobite"), but he finds a sympathetic if powerless audience in Winston Churchill.
English cricketer Len Hutton scores a record Test score of 364 runs in a match against Australia.

Lord Runciman's mission to mitigate the Sudetenland crisis begins to break down. Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain recalls Ambassador Nevile Henderson from Berlin to instruct Henderson to set up a personal meeting between Chamberlain and Adolf Hitler.

Winston Churchill, still believing France and Britain mean to honour their promises to defend Czechoslovakia against Nazi aggression, suggests in a personal note to Neville Chamberlain that His Majesty's Government may want to set up a broad international alliance, including the United States (specifically mentioning U.S. President Franklin D. Roosevelt as possibly receptive to the idea) and the S
The Times publishes a lead article which calls on Czechoslovakia to cede the Sudetenland to Germany.
Auxiliary Territorial Service, as a women's voluntary service, established.
Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain meets German Chancellor Adolf Hitler in Berchtesgaden in an attempt to negotiate an end to German expansionist policies.

Representatives of the British and French governments call on Czechoslovak President Edvard Beneš to tell him Britain and France will not fight Hitler if he decides to annex the Sudetenland by force. At home, Winston Churchill warns of grave consequences to European security if Czechoslovakia is partitioned.
The Royal Navy ordered to sea.
is launched at Clydebank; she is the largest ship in the world at this time.
Chamberlain signs the Munich Agreement and a resolution with Germany determining to resolve all future disputes between the two countries through peaceful means.

Neville Chamberlain returns to the UK from Munich, at Heston Aerodrome memorably waving the resolution signed the day earlier with Germany, and later in Downing Street giving his famous Peace for our time speech. George VI and Queen Elizabeth appear with Chamberlain on the balcony of Buckingham Palace to celebrate the agreement, a key moment in the European foreign policy of the Chamberlain minist
Picture Post magazine first published.
City Hall, Norwich, designed in the Art Deco style by C. H. James and S. R. Pierce, is opened.

At a public meeting in his parliamentary constituency of Epping, Winston Churchill narrowly survives an attempt by fellow Conservative and constituent Sir Colin Thornton-Kemsley to remove him from Parliament.
First reported "attack" of the Halifax Slasher mass hysteria incident.
Queen consort Maud of Norway (aunt of the King) dies in a nursing home in London aged 68.
Apostolic Delegation to Great Britain appointed.
First Kindertransport from Berlin to London Liverpool Street station via Harwich.
Aircraft carrier (launched by Cammell Laird in Birkenhead in 1937 under the 1934 build plan) is commissioned into the Royal Navy.
the all-time highest attendance for a British association football league game is set as 118,567 people watch Rangers beat Celtic in an "Old Firm derby" played at Ibrox Park in Glasgow.
the Irish Republican Army (IRA) begins its S-Plan bombing campaign against public utilities on the British mainland with bombs exploding in London and Manchester (where one person is killed).

"Dutch War Scare": Admiral Wilhelm Canaris of the Abwehr leaks misinformation to the effect that Germany plans to invade the Netherlands in February, with the aim of using Dutch airfields to launch a strategic bombing offensive against Britain. The "Dutch War Scare" leads to a major change in British policies towards Europe.
the IRA plants bombs at two London Underground stations, Tottenham Court Road and Leicester Square, injuring seven, two seriously.
the first Anderson shelter (a household air raid shelter) is built in London.
Borley Rectory, a reputed haunted house in Essex, is destroyed by fire.
Britain pledges support to Poland in the event of an invasion.
the Royal Armoured Corps is formed.
the Women's Royal Naval Service is re-established.
11 IRA S-Plan campaign chemical bombs explode in public conveniences in London and Birmingham.
the Military Training Act (coming into force 3 June) introduces conscription: men aged 20 and 21 must undertake six months military training.

September – the Sutton Hoo treasure – an Anglo-Saxon ship burial – is excavated. On 28 July the Sutton Hoo helmet is uncovered. The principal treasures are presented to the British Museum by the landowner, Edith Pretty, at this time its largest ever gift from a living donor.
IRA S-Plan tear gas bombs explode in two Liverpool cinemas, causing 15 injuries, with a further four bombs exploding in Coventry and two in London.
the film Goodbye, Mr. Chips is released, for which actor Robert Donat will win the Academy Award for Best Actor.
George VI and Queen Elizabeth arrive in Quebec City to begin the first-ever visit to Canada by a reigning British sovereign.
IRA S-Plan timed incendiary bombs cause fires to break out in eight hotels.
IRA S-Plan magnesium and tear gas bombs explode during Birmingham and Liverpool cinema shows.
submarine HMS Thetis sinks during trials in Liverpool Bay. 99 men are lost.
George VI and Queen Elizabeth visit New York City on the first visit to the United States by a reigning British sovereign.
IRA S-Plan letter bombs explode in London, Birmingham and Manchester postboxes and other postal facilities.
20 August – Tientsin Incident: the Imperial Japanese Army blockades British trading settlements in the north China treaty port of Tientsin.
the Women's Auxiliary Air Force is created, absorbing the forty-eight RAF companies of the Auxiliary Territorial Service which have been formed since 1938.
the Mersey Ferry stops running to Rock Ferry.
Women's Land Army re-formed to work in agriculture.
Pan American Airways Boeing 314 flying boat Yankee Clipper inaugurates the world's first heavier-than-air North Atlantic air passenger service between the United States and Britain (Southampton).
royal visit to Britannia Royal Naval College, Dartmouth, during which the young Princess Elizabeth first meets her future husband Prince Philip of Greece.
weekly transatlantic flights scheduled by Imperial Airways; suspended in September.
first personnel of the Government Code and Cypher School move to Bletchley Park.
Sir Malcolm Campbell sets the water speed record in Blue Bird K4 on Coniston Water.
2 September – most paintings from the National Gallery in London are evacuated to Wales.

as details of the previous day's Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact become public, Parliament is recalled several weeks early; the Emergency Powers (Defence) Act 1939 gives full authority to defence regulations, Army reservists are called up, Civil Defence workers are placed on alert and the government advises remaining British citizens in Germany to return home.
Royal Navy proceeds to war stations.
British Expeditionary Force headquarters formed.
World War II:
first bombing of Wilhelmshaven in World War II by Royal Air Force Vickers Wellingtons.
National Registration Act.
British Expeditionary Force crosses to France.
British submarine torpedoes and sinks another British submarine, , off the coast of Norway, believing her to be a German U-boat, with the loss of 52 crew.
the Duke of Windsor is appointed a major-general attached to the British Military Mission to France.
aircraft carrier is torpedoed and sunk by in the Western Approaches with the loss of 519 crew, the first British warship loss of the War.
American-born fascist politician William Joyce, at this time holding a British passport, begins broadcasting Nazi propaganda to Britain from Berlin, inheriting the nickname Lord Haw-Haw.
popular radio comedy show It's That Man Again with Tommy Handley first broadcast on the BBC Home service, following trial broadcasts from 12 July.
petrol rationing introduced.

flying from in the North Sea, Lieutenant B. S. McEwen of the Fleet Air Arm scores the first British victory over a German aircraft of the war, shooting down a flying boat. The aircraft carrier comes under air attack but survives.
first war tax is revealed by the Cabinet, including a significant rise in income taxes.
national register of citizens compiled to support the introduction of identity cards and rationing.
Identity cards introduced.
call-up proclamation: All men aged 20–21 must register with the military authorities.
cruiser departs Plymouth in convoy for Halifax, Nova Scotia, carrying £2M in gold bar to be used for purchase of military materiel in North America, a predecessor of Operation Fish.
HMS Royal Oak sunk by a German U-boat in Scapa Flow, Orkney Islands with the loss of 833 crew.
first enemy aircraft shot down by RAF Fighter Command, a Junkers Ju 88 brought down into the sea by Spitfires following an attack on Rosyth Naval Dockyard in Scotland.
first bomb lands in the U.K., at Hoy in the Orkney Islands.
registration of men aged 20 to 23 for National Service begins.
"Humbie Heinkel": A Heinkel He 111 bomber is the first German aircraft to be shot down on British soil by RAF Fighter Command, near Humbie in East Lothian, Scotland.

British battleship is unsuccessfully attacked by under the command of captain Wilhelm Zahn off Orkney and is hit by three torpedoes, none of which explode; Winston Churchill (First Lord of the Admiralty), Admiral of the Fleet Dudley Pound (First Sea Lord) and Admiral Charles Forbes (Commander-in-Chief Home Fleet) are on board.
Stewart Menzies is appointed head of the Secret Intelligence Service.
Venlo Incident: two British agents of SIS are captured by the Germans.
British armed merchantman is sunk in the GIUK gap in an action against the German battleships and .
British Overseas Airways Corporation formed by merger of Imperial Airways and British Airways Ltd. effective from 1 April 1940.
first soldier of the British Expeditionary Force killed: Corporal Thomas Priday triggers a French land mine.
escorting destroyer sinks after a collision with battleship off the Mull of Kintyre in heavy fog with the loss of 124 men.
the Battle of the River Plate takes place between , , and the German cruiser Admiral Graf Spee, forcing the latter to scuttle herself on 17 December.
Battle of the Heligoland Bight: RAF Bomber Command, on a daylight mission to attack Kriegsmarine ships in the Heligoland Bight, is repulsed by Luftwaffe fighter aircraft.
the Pilgrim Trust establishes a Committee for the Encouragement of Music and the Arts, predecessor of the Arts Council.
World War II: Britain calls up 2,000,000 19- to 27-year-olds for military service.

Unity Mitford, daughter of David Freeman-Mitford, 2nd Baron Redesdale, and fervent admirer of Adolf Hitler, having attempted suicide, returns to England from Germany (via Switzerland); she is carried down the gangplank of the cross-channel ferry at Folkestone on a stretcher.
Oliver Stanley replaces Leslie Hore-Belisha as Secretary of State for War.
The BBC Forces Programme begins broadcasting; it becomes the most popular channel among civilians at home as well as its primary target audience.
Food rationing is introduced; it will remain in force until 1954.
World War II: liner Dunbar Castle of the Union Castle Line hits a mine in the English Channel and sinks with the loss of 9 men (2 dead and 7 missing).
A wave of freezing weather afflicting most of Europe leads to the River Thames freezing for the first time since 1888.
Explosion at Waltham Abbey Royal Gunpowder Mills (five killed).
Severe ice storm across the UK.
Altmark incident: Royal Navy destroyer pursues German tanker Altmark into the neutral waters of the Jøssingfjorden in southwestern Norway and frees the 290 British seamen held aboard.
The last mounted charge by a British cavalry regiment is made when the Royal Scots Greys are called to quell Arab rioters in Mandatory Palestine.
British battleship is torpedoed by a U-boat but suffers only minor damage.

Frisch–Peierls memorandum: Otto Frisch and Rudolf Peierls, at this time working at the University of Birmingham, calculate that an atomic bomb could be produced using very much less enriched uranium than has previously been supposed, making it a practical proposition.
makes her maiden voyage from Clydebank to New York.
Rationing of meat introduced.

Indian nationalist Udham Singh assassinates Sir Michael O'Dwyer (in revenge for the 1919 Jallianwala Bagh massacre) at Caxton Hall in London, for which he is hanged on 31 July at HM Prison Pentonville.
First civilian casualty of bombing in the UK, on Orkney.
Last terrorist bomb in the Irish Republican Army's S-Plan campaign on the British mainland (and until 1973) explodes harmlessly on a London rubbish dump.
Old Age and Widows' Pensions Act reduces the pensionable age for insured women and the wives of pensioned men from 65 to 60.
A metallic security thread is added to £1 notes to prevent forgeries.
33 fascist sympathisers are interned.
British Overseas Airways Corporation begins operation as a single company.
Neville Chamberlain declares in a public speech that Hitler has "missed the bus".
British campaign in Norway commences following Operation Weserübung, the German invasion of neutral Denmark and Norway.
MAUD Committee first convened to consider the feasibility of an atomic bomb.
British occupation of the Faroe Islands, following the German invasion of Denmark, to avert a possible German occupation of the islands.
The War Budget sees the introduction of Purchase Tax and an increase in tobacco duties.
Last British and French troops evacuated from Norway following failure in the Norwegian Campaign.
Norway Debate in the House of Commons. Strong opposition to the Chamberlain ministry's conduct of the war make it impossible for him to continue as Prime Minister.
Recruitment begins for a home defence force – the Local Defence Volunteers, renamed as the Home Guard from 23 July.
Large-scale alien internment begins.
Parliament passes the Emergency Powers (Defence) Act 1940, giving the government full control over all persons and property.
Anglo-French Supreme War Council decides to withdraw all forces under its control from Norway.
4 June – The Dunkirk evacuation of British Expeditionary Force takes place. 300,000 troops are evacuated from France to England.
May 1940 War Cabinet Crisis: Churchill wins the War Cabinet round to his view that there should be no peace negotiations with Hitler, contrary to the view of his Foreign Secretary, Viscount Halifax.
Secretary of State for War Anthony Eden gives a radio address claiming success of the Dunkirk evacuation.
Churchill makes his We shall fight on the beaches speech to the House of Commons.
Novelist J. B. Priestley broadcasts his first Sunday evening radio Postscript, "An Excursion to Hell", on the BBC Home Service, marking the role of the pleasure steamers in the Dunkirk evacuation.
King Haakon VII of Norway and his government are evacuated to London on HMS Devonshire.
The Commandos are created.
Italy declares war on France and the United Kingdom.
The Western Desert campaign opens with British forces crossing the Frontier Wire into Italian Libya.
Over 10,000 soldiers of the 51st (Highland) Division under General Victor Fortune surrender to Rommel at Saint-Valery-en-Caux.

The Churchill war ministry offers a Franco-British Union (inspired by Jean Monnet) to Paul Reynaud, Prime Minister of France, in the hope of preventing France from agreeing to an armistice with Nazi Germany, but Reynaud resigns when his own cabinet refuses to accept it.

, serving as a troopship, is bombed and sunk by the Luftwaffe while evacuating British troops and nationals from Saint-Nazaire with the loss of at least 4,000 lives, the largest single UK loss in any World War II event, immediate news of which is suppressed in the British press. Destroyer rescues around 600.
BBC Forces Programme begins broadcasting Music While You Work.

1 July – Operation Fish: Royal Navy cruiser sails from Greenock in convoy to Halifax, Nova Scotia, carrying a large part of the gold reserves of the United Kingdom and securities for safe keeping in Canada. Another convoy sets sail on 5 July from the Clyde, including HMS Batory, carrying cargo worth $1.7 billion, the largest movement of wealth in history.
German forces land in Guernsey, start of the 5-year Occupation of the Channel Islands.
First Luftwaffe daylight bombing raid on mainland Britain at Wick, Caithness: 15 civilians, 8 of them children, are killed.
British-owned , carrying civilian internees and POWs of Italian and German origin from Liverpool to Canada, is torpedoed and sunk by off northwest Ireland with the loss of around 865 lives.
Special Operations Executive formed to undertake espionage and sabotage in enemy-occupied countries.
Birmingham Blitz (Regenschirm): Heavy bombing of Birmingham begins.
Adlertag ("Eagle Day") strike on southern England occurs, starting the rapid escalation of the Battle of Britain.
Churchill pays tribute in Parliament to the Royal Air Force fighter crews: "Never in the field of human conflict was so much owed by so many to so few."
Allied Forces Act 1940 gives authority for governments in exile in the UK to maintain their independent troops on British soil.
RAF bombing of Berlin begins.
Texel Disaster: Two Royal Navy destroyers are sunk by running into a minefield off the coast of the occupied Netherlands with the loss of around 400 men, 300 of them dead.

Destroyers for Bases Agreement between the United Kingdom and United States is announced, to the effect that 50 U.S. destroyers needed for escort work will be transferred to Britain. In return, the United States gains 99-year leases on British bases in the North Atlantic, West Indies and Bermuda.
Adolf Hitler's Winterhilfe speech at the Berlin Sportpalast declares that Nazi Germany will make retaliatory night air raids on British cities and threatens invasion.
A bomb at South Hallsville School, Canning Town in the East End of London, which is in use as an evacuation centre, kills at least 77 and perhaps four times as many.
Churchill, speaking from the Cabinet War Rooms, warns of a possible German invasion.
Buckingham Palace is damaged by the Luftwaffe in an air raid. The King and Queen survive without injury and inspect the damage.
RAF command claims victory over the Luftwaffe in the Battle of Britain; this day is thereafter known as "Battle of Britain Day".
Hitler postpones Operation Sea Lion (Unternehmen Seelöwe), the planned German invasion of Britain, indefinitely.

is torpedoed by in the Atlantic with the loss of 248 of the 406 on board, including child evacuees bound for Canada. The sinking results in cancellation of the Children's Overseas Reception Board's plan to relocate British children abroad.
King George VI announces the creation of the George Cross decoration during a radio broadcast.

Battle of Graveney Marsh in Kent, the last exchange of shots with a foreign force on mainland British soil, takes place when soldiers of the London Irish Rifles capture the crew of a downed new German Junkers Ju 88 bomber who initially resist arrest with gunfire; one of the enemy is shot in the foot.
Winston Churchill succeeds Neville Chamberlain as Leader of the Conservative Party.
At least 66 people are killed when a German bomb penetrates Balham station on the London Underground which is in use as an air-raid shelter.
Purchase Tax is introduced, initially on luxury goods at 33.33%.
The Belgian government in exile, having been dispersed in France, Spain and Switzerland, regroups in London.
Air Chief Marshal Sir Charles Portal is appointed to succeed Sir Cyril Newall as Chief of the Air Staff, a post he will hold for the remainder of the War.
Cryptanalysis of the Enigma messages at Bletchley Park confirms that a German invasion will not be taking place.
The Battle of Britain ends.

Allied Convoy HX 84 is attacked by German cruiser Admiral Scheer in the North Atlantic; the sacrifice of escorting British armed merchant cruiser under Capt. Edward Fegen and enables a majority of the ships (including tanker ) to escape.
Fourteen children are killed when a German bomb hits the Civic Centre in Southampton.
Major fire at Castle Howard in Yorkshire (at this time housing an evacuated girls' school).
Battle of Taranto: the Royal Navy launches the first aircraft carrier strike in history, on the Italian fleet at Taranto.

Coventry Blitz: the centre of Coventry is destroyed by 500 German Luftwaffe bombers: 150,000 incendiary devices, 503 tons of high explosives and 130 parachute mines level 60,000 of the city's 75,000 buildings. At least 568 people are killed, while 863 more are injured. Exceptionally, the location and nature of the damage here is immediately publicised in the media.

Less than a week after the blitz of Coventry, further heavy air raids take place in central England. Birmingham, West Bromwich, Dudley and Tipton are all bombed. Some 900 people are killed and 2,000 more injured – there are 53 deaths at the Birmingham Small Arms Company factory in Small Heath alone. Most of the region's casualties are in Birmingham.
Southampton Blitz: Southampton is bombed.
Bristol Blitz: beginning of the bombing of Bristol.
1 December – Oil storage depot fire at Turnchapel, Plymouth, caused by bombing.
Liverpool Blitz: a parachute mine hitting a basement shelter in Edge Hill, Liverpool, kills 166.
Sheffield Blitz ("Operation Crucible"): the city of Sheffield is heavily bombed by the Luftwaffe. 660 people are killed, while another 1,500 are injured and 30,000 more left homeless.

Release of the Ealing Studios war comedy Sailors Three, starring Tommy Trinder, Claude Hulbert and Michael Wilding; the song "All Over The Place", sung by Trinder in the film (words by Frank Eyton; music by Noel Gay), becomes one of the most popular of the war.
An anti-aircraft shell fired from Dudley accidentally strikes a public house in neighbouring Tipton, resulting in dozens of casualties.
Liverpool Blitz: Liverpool is heavily bombed, with well over 300 people killed and hundreds more injured.
Manchester Blitz: Manchester is heavily bombed as the Luftwaffe air raids on Britain continue. 363 are killed and 1,183 wounded; and Manchester Cathedral is badly damaged.
Heavy bombing in London causes the Second Great Fire of London. Guildhall is among many buildings badly damaged or destroyed. There are hundreds more casualties.
